questions.question: A data file consisting of 1,50,000 student-records is stored on a hard disk with block size of 4096 bytes. The data file is sorted on the primary key RollNo. The size of a record pointer for this disk is 7 bytes. Each student-record has a candidate key attribute called ANum of size 12 bytes. Suppose an index file with records consisting of two fields, ANum value and the record pointer the corresponding student record, is built and stored on the same disk. Assume that the records of data file and index file are not split across disk blocks. The number of blocks in the index file is ______
questions.explanation:
ANum is not the sorting key, so the index must be dense: one entry per record.

Entry size = 12 + 7 = 19 bytes [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] entries per block = [latex]\lfloor4096/19\rfloor=215[/latex].
Blocks = [latex]\lceil150000/215\rceil=698[/latex]

Answer: 698

questions.question:
Consider the following two tables and four queries in SQL.

Which one of the queries above is certain to have an output that is a superset of the outputs of the other three queries?

options.A: Query 1
options.B: Query 2
options.C: Query 3
options.D: Query 4

questions.explanation:
Checking each statement:
- Query 1 (inner join): matching rows only.
- Query 2 (left outer): matching rows + unmatched Book rows.
- Query 3 (right outer): matching rows + unmatched Stock rows.
- Query 4 (full outer): matching rows + unmatched rows from both sides, so it always contains the other three.

Answer: Query 4

questions.question:
Suppose a database system crashes again while recovering from a previous crash. Assume checkpointing is not done by the database either during the transactions or during recovery.

Which of the following statements is/are correct?

options.A: The same undo and redo list will be used while recovering again
options.B: The system cannot recover any further
options.C: All the transactions that are already undone and redone will not be recovered again
options.D: The database will become inconsistent

questions.explanation:
Without checkpoints, recovery always starts from the log. Undo and redo are idempotent (doing them again gives the same result), so after a second crash the same undo and redo lists are built from the log and applied again.

The database can still recover and stays consistent.

Answer: The same undo and redo list will be used while recovering again

questions.question: Suppose  a database schedule S involves transactions T1,...,Tn. Construct the precedence graph of S with vertices representing the transactions and edges representing the conflicts. If S is serializable, which one of the following orderings of the vertices of the precedence graph is guaranteed to yield a serial schedule?

options.A: Topological order
options.B: Depth-first order
options.C: Breadth-first order
options.D: Ascending orderoftransactionindices

questions.explanation:
Each edge [latex]T_i\rightarrow T_j[/latex] means [latex]T_i[/latex] must come first. A serializable schedule has an acyclic precedence graph, and any topological order respects every edge, so it gives an equivalent serial schedule.

Answer: Topological order

questions.question:
In an Entity-Relationship (ER) model, suppose R is a many-to-one relationship from entity set E1 to entity set E2. Assume that E1 and E2 participate totally in R and that the cardinality of E1 is greater than the cardinality of E2.
Which one of the following is true about R?

options.A: Every entity in E1 is associated with exactly one entity in E2.
options.B: Some entity in E1 is associated with more than one entity in E2.
options.C: Every entity in E2 is associated with exactly one entity in E1.
options.D: Every entity in E2 is associated with at most one entity in E1.

questions.explanation:
Many-to-one from E1 to E2 means each E1 entity relates to at most one E2 entity; total participation of E1 makes it at least one. So every E1 entity is associated with exactly one E2 entity. Since E1 is larger, E2 entities may have several E1 partners.

Answer: Every entity in E1 is associated with exactly one entity in E2

questions.question:
Consider the following three relations in a relational database.
[latex]Employee(eId, Name), Brand (bId, bName), Own(eId ,bId)[/latex]
Which of the following relational algebra expressions return the set of [latex]eIds[/latex] who own all the brands?

options.A: [latex]  \Pi _{eId}(\Pi _{eId,bId}(Own)/\Pi _{bId}(Brand))[/latex]
options.B: [latex]  \Pi _{eId}(Own)-\Pi _{eId}\left ((\Pi _{eId}(Own) \times \Pi _{bId}(Brand) )-\Pi _{eId,bId}(Own)  \right )[/latex]
options.C: [latex]\Pi _{eId}(\Pi _{eId,bId}(Own)/\Pi _{bId}(Own))  [/latex]
options.D: [latex] \Pi _{eId}\left ((\Pi _{eId}(Own) \times \Pi _{bId}(Own) )/\Pi _{bId}(Brand)  \right ) [/latex]

questions.explanation:
"Owns all brands" is relational division by the set of all brands.

- Option 1: [latex]\Pi_{eId,bId}(Own)\div\Pi_{bId}(Brand)[/latex] [latex]\text{---}[/latex] exactly division [latex]\text{---}[/latex] TRUE.
- Option 2: [latex]\Pi_{eId}(Own)\times\Pi_{bId}(Brand)[/latex] lists every (employee, brand) pair; subtracting Own leaves the pairs an employee does not own. Removing those employees leaves those who own every brand [latex]\text{---}[/latex] TRUE (this is the expansion of division).
- Option 3 divides by [latex]\Pi_{bId}(Own)[/latex] (brands owned by someone); a brand owned by nobody would be ignored [latex]\text{---}[/latex] wrong.
- Option 4 divides a full cross product, which returns every employee [latex]\text{---}[/latex] wrong.

Answer: Options 1 and 2

questions.question:
Which of the following statements about a relation R in first normal form (1NF)
is/are TRUE ?

options.A: R can have a multi-attribute key
options.B: R cannot have a foreign key
options.C: R cannot have a composite attribute
options.D: R cannot have more than one candidate key

questions.explanation:
1NF only requires every attribute value to be atomic (no multi-valued or composite attributes).

- R can have a multi-attribute key [latex]\text{---}[/latex] TRUE (e.g. key (roll_no, course_id)). This is about keys, not about values.
- R cannot have a foreign key [latex]\text{---}[/latex] FALSE, 1NF puts no restriction on foreign keys.
- R cannot have a composite attribute [latex]\text{---}[/latex] TRUE, a composite attribute is non-atomic and must be split into simple attributes.
- R cannot have more than one candidate key [latex]\text{---}[/latex] FALSE.

Answer: R can have a multi-attribute key; R cannot have a composite attribute

questions.question:
Consider a database of fixed-length records, stored as an ordered file. The database has 25,000 records, with each record being 100 bytes, of which the primary key occupies 15 bytes. The data file is block-aligned in that each data record is fully contained within a block. The database is indexed by a primary index file, which is also stored as a block-aligned ordered file. The figure below depicts this indexing scheme.

Suppose the block size of the file system is 1024 bytes, and a pointer to a block occupies 5 bytes. The system uses binary search on the index file to search for a record with a given key. You may assume that a binary search on an index file of [latex]b[/latex] blocks takes [latex]\left \lceil \log_2 b \right \rceil [/latex] block accesses in the worst case.
Given a key, the number of block accesses required to identify the block in the data file that may contain a record with the key, in the worst case, is _____
questions.explanation:
Compute the index size step by step:
- Records per data block = [latex]\lfloor1024/100\rfloor=10[/latex] [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] data blocks = 25000 / 10 = 2500.
- Primary (sparse) index has one entry per data block: 2500 entries of [latex]15+5=20[/latex] bytes.
- Entries per index block = [latex]\lfloor1024/20\rfloor=51[/latex] [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] index blocks = [latex]\lceil2500/51\rceil=50[/latex].

Binary search on the index: [latex]\lceil\log_2 50\rceil=6[/latex] block accesses identify the data block.

Answer: 6

questions.question:
SQL allows duplicate tuples in relations, and correspondingly defines the multiplicity of tuples in the result of joins. Which one of the following queries always gives the same answer as the nested query shown below:
Select * from R where a in (select S. a from S)

options.A: Select R. * from R, S where R. a=S. a
options.B: Select distinct R. * from R,S where R. a=S. a
options.C: Select R. * from R, (select distinct a from S) as S1 where R. a=S1.a
options.D: Select R. * from R, S where R.a = S. a and is unique R

questions.explanation:
The IN query returns each R tuple once per its own copy in R, no matter how many matching tuples S has.

- Option 1: a plain join repeats an R tuple once for every matching S tuple [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] extra duplicates.
- Option 2: DISTINCT also removes duplicates that were genuinely in R.
- Option 3: S1 has each value of a only once, so every R tuple matches at most once [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] same result.

Answer: Select R.* from R, (select distinct a from S) as S1 where R.a = S1.a

questions.question: The symbol [latex] \rightarrow [/latex] indicates functional dependency in the context of a relational database. Which of the following options is/are TRUE?

options.A: [latex] (X, Y) \rightarrow(Z, W) \text { implies } X \rightarrow(Z, W)  [/latex]
options.B: [latex] (X, Y) \rightarrow(Z, W) \text { implies }(X, Y) \rightarrow Z  [/latex]
options.C: [latex] ((X, Y) \rightarrow Z \text { and } W \rightarrow Y) \text { implies }(X, W) \rightarrow Z  [/latex]
options.D: [latex] (X \rightarrow Y \text { and } Y \rightarrow Z) \text { implies } X \rightarrow Z [/latex]

questions.explanation:
Checking each statement:
- [latex](X,Y)\rightarrow(Z,W)[/latex] does not give [latex]X\rightarrow(Z,W)[/latex]; Y may be required [latex]\text{---}[/latex] FALSE.
- Decomposition rule: [latex]XY\rightarrow ZW[/latex] [latex]\Rightarrow[/latex] [latex]XY\rightarrow Z[/latex] [latex]\text{---}[/latex] TRUE.
- Pseudo-transitivity: [latex]W\rightarrow Y[/latex] [latex]\Rightarrow[/latex] [latex]XW\rightarrow XY[/latex] (augment by X), and [latex]XY\rightarrow Z[/latex], so [latex]XW\rightarrow Z[/latex] [latex]\text{---}[/latex] TRUE.
- Transitivity: [latex]X\rightarrow Y,\;Y\rightarrow Z[/latex] [latex]\Rightarrow[/latex] [latex]X\rightarrow Z[/latex] [latex]\text{---}[/latex] TRUE.

Answer: Options 2, 3 and 4

questions.question:
The relation schema, Person(pid,city), describes the city of residence for every person uniquely identified by pid. The following relational algebra operators are available: selection, projection, cross product, and rename.

questions.question:
Let [latex]r_i(z)[/latex] and [latex]w_i(z)[/latex] denote read and write operations respectively on a data item [latex]z[/latex] by a transaction [latex]T_i[/latex]. Consider the following two schedules.

[latex]S1: r_1(x)r_1(y)r_2(x)r_2(y)w_2(y)w_1(x)[/latex]
[latex]S2: r_1(x)r_2(x)r_2(y)w_2(y)r_1(y)w_1(x)[/latex]

Which one of the following options is correct?

options.A: S1 is conflict serializable, and S2 is not conflict serializable
options.B: S1 is not conflict serializable, and S2 is conflict serializable
options.C: Both S1 and S2 are conflict serializable
options.D: Niether S1 nor S2 is conflict serializable

questions.explanation:
S1: [latex]r_1(y)[/latex] before [latex]w_2(y)[/latex] gives T1 [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] T2; [latex]r_2(x)[/latex] before [latex]w_1(x)[/latex] gives T2 [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] T1. Cycle [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] not conflict serializable.

S2: [latex]r_2(x)[/latex] before [latex]w_1(x)[/latex] gives T2 [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] T1; [latex]w_2(y)[/latex] before [latex]r_1(y)[/latex] gives T2 [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] T1. No cycle [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] conflict serializable (T2, T1).

Answer: S1 is not conflict serializable, and S2 is conflict serializable

questions.question:
Consider the database transactions [latex]T1 [/latex] and [latex]T2 [/latex], and data items [latex]X [/latex] and [latex]Y [/latex]. Which of the schedule(s) is/are conflict serializable?

[latex] \begin{array}{|l|} \hline \textbf{Transaction T1} \\ \hline R1(X) \\ \hline W1(Y) \\ \hline R1(X) \\ \hline W1(X) \\ \hline \text{COMMIT(T1)} \\ \hline \end{array} [/latex]

[latex] \begin{array}{|l|} \hline \textbf{Transaction T2} \\ \hline W2(X) \\ \hline W2(Y) \\ \hline \text{COMMIT(T2)} \\ \hline \end{array} [/latex]

options.A: [latex]R1(X), W2(X), W1(Y), W2(Y), R1(X), W1(X), \text{COMMIT}(T2), \text{COMMIT}(T1) [/latex]
options.B: [latex]W2(X), R1(X), W2(Y), W1(Y), R1(X), \text{COMMIT}(T2), W1(X), \text{COMMIT}(T1) [/latex]
options.C: [latex]R1(X), W1(Y), W2(X), W2(Y), R1(X), W1(X), \text{COMMIT}(T1), \text{COMMIT}(T2) [/latex]
options.D: [latex]W2(X), R1(X), W1(Y), W2(Y), R1(X), \text{COMMIT}(T2), W1(X), \text{COMMIT}(T1) [/latex]

questions.explanation:
Build the conflict/precedence graph for each schedule (an edge [latex]T_i\to T_j[/latex] whenever an operation of [latex]T_i[/latex] on some data item precedes a conflicting operation of [latex]T_j[/latex] on the same item, with at least one being a write); the schedule is conflict serializable iff this graph has no cycle.

Checking [latex]R1(X),W2(X),W1(Y),W2(Y),R1(X),W1(X),\ldots[/latex]: the first [latex]R1(X)[/latex] before [latex]W2(X)[/latex] gives [latex]T1\to T2[/latex], but the later [latex]R1(X)[/latex] appearing after [latex]W2(X)[/latex] gives [latex]T2\to T1[/latex] — a cycle. Not serializable.

Checking [latex]W2(X),R1(X),W2(Y),W1(Y),R1(X),\ldots,W1(X),\ldots[/latex]: every conflicting pair consistently gives [latex]T2\to T1[/latex] (write-then-read on [latex]X[/latex] first, write-then-write on [latex]Y[/latex], and the final [latex]W1(X)[/latex] happens safely after [latex]T2[/latex] has already committed) — no cycle. Conflict serializable.

The other two schedules can be checked the same way and each produces a cycle (conflicting edges pointing in both directions between T1 and T2).

Answer: Only "W2(X), R1(X), W2(Y), W1(Y), R1(X), COMMIT(T2), W1(X), COMMIT(T1)" is conflict serializable.
